title: 2. What the Company Does: Segments, Revenue Mix & Concrete Examples

epigraph.quote: A refractory lining is a tiny fraction of a steelmaker's bill of materials, yet it governs the single largest variable in melt-shop economics: furnace availability.
epigraph.author: Industrial Metallurgy Principle

web_blocks.html: RPEL supplies specialized refractory consumables and engineered mineral products [2][3][25]. Its core product is silica ramming mass for coreless induction furnaces, alongside high-purity quartz powder, tundish boards and continuous-casting accessories, and custom foundry mixes [2][3][25]. Unlike capital equipment bought once a decade, ramming mass is a recurring melt-shop consumable [9]. Industry benchmarks show secondary steel producers use roughly 30 kg of ramming mass per tonne of steel produced [9]. Mills must reline each furnace every few days or weeks based on scrap quality and melt temperature [9].

web_blocks.takeaway: RPEL's product portfolio is engineered around circular material efficiency—from premium boron-oxide premixes down to turning silica dust fines into tundish boards.

web_blocks.html: A quick melt-shop example shows why mills switch from unorganized local vendors to RPEL. In a 15-tonne coreless induction furnace, workers pour dry silica ramming mass between a sacrificial steel former and the coil insulation [12]. They then vibrate the dry mass to reach maximum bulk density [12]. As the first charge heats past 500°C–700°C, the minor boron additive (0.8%–2.0%) reacts with silica grains to form a viscous borosilicate glass phase [12]. This reaction sinters the inner face into a dense ceramic crucible, while the outer layer stays loose to absorb thermal expansion [12].

Unorganized grinders often supply uneven grain sizes or let iron impurities slip past weak magnets. Those impurities lower the lining's melting point and cause early spalling after 12–15 heats. RPEL solves this with RM 9901 Premix Boron, an in-house blend built with boron oxide sourced from global suppliers such as Rio Tinto Borax [12][26]. The premix removes manual boric-acid dosing errors on the factory floor [12][26]. Even 3 to 5 extra heats per lining save a mill far more in power, labor, and uptime than RPEL's price premium per tonne [21].

Commercially, RPEL has shifted steadily toward higher-value exports and engineered grades [21][22]. In FY25, exports reached 30% of total sales volume at 76,645 MT, up 25% YoY from 61,480 MT [21]. By FY26, consolidated revenue hit ₹257 Cr across 39–40 destination countries in the Middle East, Africa, South Asia, and Europe [22]. Export realizations jumped sharply as standalone export turnover reached ₹55.54 Cr, or ~48.59% of standalone sales [22]. Over this arc, RPEL's EBITDA per metric tonne more than doubled from roughly ₹1,245/MT in FY17 to ~₹2,650/MT by Q1 FY27, proving real mix-led pricing power [2][23].

Beyond furnace linings, RPEL's move into Tundish Boards and continuous-casting consumables (garpack, garseal, and nozzle-filling compounds) creates a second revenue stream with zero raw-material friction [25]. Crushing quartz into tight ramming-mass grades always produces ultra-fine silica dust [25]. RPEL feeds those plant fines straight into its Newai tundish board line, turning a disposal cost into specialty margins [25].

web_blocks.title: Circular Economics: Waste-to-Tundish Boards
paragraphs: Crushing quartz into tight ramming-mass grades always creates ultra-fine silica dust [25]. Instead of dumping those fines at a loss, RPEL built a dedicated Newai plant to turn plant waste into Tundish Boards, garpack, garseal, and nozzle-filling compounds [25]. This circular loop cuts unit waste while lifting consolidated gross margins [25].

book_paragraphs: Let's step onto the melt-shop floor for a moment, because you cannot evaluate Raghav Productivity Enhancers from a spreadsheet alone without seeing what happens inside a fifteen-tonne coreless induction furnace. Imagine a giant cylindrical pot wrapped in water-cooled copper coils carrying massive electrical currents. Inside that pot, scrap steel and sponge iron are heated past 1,600 degrees Celsius until they turn into a glowing liquid bath.

What stands between that 1,600-degree molten steel and the copper coils? Not a thick brick wall, as you might picture in a blast furnace, but a dry, granular blanket of silica ramming mass—barely a few inches thick—packed tightly around a sacrificial steel template. As the furnace fires up for its first heat, something remarkable happens between 500 and 700 degrees Celsius. A tiny 1% pinch of boron additive melts and reacts with the ultra-pure quartz grains to form a thin, viscous borosilicate glass bond. The inner face sinters into a rock-hard ceramic crucible, while the outer layer stays semi-loose to cushion thermal expansion.

book_subsections.title: Why RM 9901 and Foundry Grades Command Pricing Power
paragraphs: Now consider the steelmaker's math. A secondary steel mill consumes roughly thirty kilograms of ramming mass for every tonne of steel it pours. The ramming mass itself is a tiny sliver of total steelmaking cost. Yet if a cheap, unorganized local mix has uneven grain sizes or stray iron particles, the lining erodes unevenly and forces a shutdown after a dozen heats. Every unscheduled relining costs hours of lost melting time, wasted electricity, and dangerous manual labor.

That is why RPEL's flagship RM 9901 Premix Boron—which replaces manual shop-floor boric acid mixing with factory-premixed boron oxide—became such a sticky product. When a mill gets three to five extra heats per lining and zero mixing errors, it stops haggling over a few hundred rupees per tonne. Add in the foundry-grade formulations developed with Jan W. Kjellberg for precision ductile iron and alloy steel castings, and you begin to see why customers rarely switch back once qualified.

book_subsections.title: Circular Material Economics and Export Realizations
paragraphs: What makes RPEL's product architecture even cleverer is how it monetizes every fraction of the quartz rock it crushes. High-purity ramming mass requires a very specific particle-size curve, which naturally leaves behind ultra-fine silica dust. Instead of treating those fines as quarry waste, RPEL built a plant in Newai to press them into tundish boards, garpack, garseal, and nozzle-filling compounds used in continuous casting. Even the dust gets sold at specialty margins.

You can see the financial fingerprint of this product mix shift in two numbers. First, export volumes grew 25% in FY25 to 76,645 metric tonnes, representing 30% of total volume, and by FY26 RPEL was shipping to nearly forty countries with standalone export turnover approaching 49% of standalone sales. Second, EBITDA per metric tonne climbed from roughly ₹1,245 back in FY17 to around ₹2,650 by Q1 FY27. That is not the trajectory of a company selling commodity sand; it is the signature of a specialized consumable franchise.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: When a consumable represents a small fraction of a customer's cost structure but governs plant uptime and safety, switching costs are operational, not contractual. That is the core of RPEL's pricing power.
